title: BEFORE JETHRO BECAME MOSES’ FATHER-IN-LAW, HE WAS SOMEONE THE BIBLE DOESN’T WANT YOU TO OVERLOOK
paragraphs: BEFORE JETHRO BECAME MOSES’ FATHER-IN-LAW, HE WAS SOMEONE THE BIBLE DOESN’T WANT YOU TO OVERLOOK
The mysterious priest of Midian, seven daughters at a well, a fugitive carrying the weight of murder, and the extraordinary way God was preparing a deliverer through a family nobody expected.
What if one of the most important people God used to prepare Moses for his calling was a man who did not belong to Israel?
Not Abraham.
Not Isaac.
Not Jacob.
Not even one of the elders of Israel.
A priest from Midian.
A father of seven daughters.
A man living far from Egypt, far from Pharaoh's palace, and far from the suffering of the Hebrew slaves.
His name was Jethro.

But before Moses ever called him his father-in-law, before Jethro offered counsel that would help Moses lead an entire nation, and before Scripture recorded him acknowledging the greatness of the LORD, this man already had a history.
A household.
A religious identity.
A place in a world that Moses had never imagined becoming part of.
And perhaps the most surprising thing about Jethro's story is not what Scripture tells us.
It is what Scripture deliberately leaves unanswered.
Because if we are going to understand this man, we must resist the temptation to invent a dramatic conversion story, manufacture a scandal, or pretend we know details God never revealed.
The truth Scripture actually gives us is powerful enough.
And somewhere in this ancient story is a message for the person who feels that one terrible chapter has disqualified them from ever being useful to God again.
But first, we need to go back to Egypt.
Back to the moment Moses lost everything.
Moses had grown up in extraordinary circumstances.
Born a Hebrew during a time when Pharaoh commanded the death of Hebrew baby boys, he was preserved through the courage of his mother and eventually raised in Pharaoh's household (Exodus 2:1–10).
He had access to privilege while his own people suffered under oppression.
Then came the moment that changed his life.
He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew.
He looked around.
He struck the Egyptian.
And the Egyptian died.
Exodus 2:12 says Moses hid the body in the sand.
Think about that.
The man who would one day stand before Pharaoh declaring God's command to release Israel was now hiding evidence of a killing.
The future deliverer was not standing in triumph.
He was standing over a buried body.
When the matter became known, Pharaoh sought to kill him.
Moses fled.
And suddenly, the palace was behind him.
The security was gone.
The familiar world had collapsed.
He was no longer living as a privileged member of Egypt's royal household.
He was a fugitive in a foreign land.
Scripture tells us that Moses fled to Midian and sat down beside a well.
And this is where Jethro's story enters.
Not with thunder.
Not with a heavenly announcement.
Not with a burning bush.
With a well.
With thirsty animals.
With seven daughters trying to do their work.
And with an exhausted stranger who had no idea how deeply his life was about to change.
Exodus 2:16 introduces the man who would become Moses' father-in-law with a remarkably simple description.
The Hebrew reads:
וּלְכֹהֵן מִדְיָן שֶׁבַע בָּנוֹת
Ulekhōhēn Midyān sheva banōt.
A close translation is:
“Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters.”
Notice what the text establishes before it tells us anything about Moses marrying into this family.
This man was already a priest.
He was already a father.
He was already an established figure in Midian.
His importance did not begin when Moses entered his household.
And that matters.
The Hebrew word כֹּהֵן (kōhēn) means “priest,” a person associated with religious service and sacred duties.
The text identifies him as a priest of Midian, but it does not explicitly tell us which deity he served at that earlier point in his life.
That distinction is important.
Some readers assume Jethro must have been an idol worshiper who later converted to the worship of Israel's God.
Others argue that he may already have possessed knowledge of the true God.
The biblical text does not give us enough information to establish either conclusion with certainty.
Midian was a region and a people with connections to Abraham's wider family.
Genesis 25:1–4 identifies Midian as a son of Abraham through Keturah.
This means that the Midianites were not entirely disconnected from the ancestral world of Abraham.
Yet shared ancestry does not prove shared faith.
And being a priest does not automatically establish that Jethro was a priest of the LORD.
What we can say is that Jethro occupied a recognized religious position in Midian before he became connected to Moses.
He was not introduced as a king.
Not as a military commander.
Not as a prophet receiving direct revelation.
He was introduced as a priest with seven daughters.
And those daughters were about to become the unexpected doorway through which Moses would enter his household.
One day, they came to the well to draw water for their father's flock.
But other shepherds arrived and drove them away.
Imagine the frustration.
The women had come to perform a necessary task.
They had drawn water.
They were trying to care for their animals.
Then stronger shepherds pushed them aside.
Scripture does not tell us whether this had happened before. We should not assume a history the passage does not describe.
But on this particular day, something different happened.
A stranger stood up.
Moses.
The same man who had fled Egypt after killing an Egyptian was now in a foreign land, intervening when he saw others being mistreated.
Exodus 2:17 records that Moses helped the daughters and watered their flock.
There is something deeply revealing here.
Moses had failed terribly in Egypt.
His attempt to intervene in oppression had ended in death and exile.
Yet his moral failure did not erase his capacity to recognize injustice.
He still saw vulnerable people being pushed aside.
He still acted.
That does not excuse his earlier killing.
It does not turn violence into righteousness.
It shows us a complicated man whose story was not finished.
And perhaps that is where this ancient account begins to reach into our own lives.
Because some people believe their worst decision has become their permanent identity.
They remember what they did.
The lie.
The betrayal.
The addiction they kept hiding.
The anger that wounded someone they loved.
The relationship they destroyed.
The opportunity they wasted.
The season when they knew what was right but chose otherwise.
And now, whenever they imagine God using them, something inside whispers:
“You already ruined your chance.”
But Moses' story confronts that despair.
God did not call Moses' killing good.
God did not erase the reality of what happened.
Yet God was not finished with Moses.
The fugitive at the well would one day become the servant through whom God confronted Pharaoh.
And one of the people who would help shape his life was waiting just beyond that well.
When Jethro's daughters returned home earlier than expected, their father was surprised.
Exodus 2:18 introduces him by another name:
רְעוּאֵל (Reʿuʾēl)
Usually rendered Reuel.
The name is commonly understood as meaning “friend of God” or “God is a friend.”
But we need to be careful.
A name containing a reference to God does not, by itself, prove the personal spiritual condition of the person bearing it.
Names can preserve family traditions, cultural beliefs, and religious language without telling us everything about an individual's faith.
There is also a question readers often overlook.
Was Reuel the same person as Jethro?
Exodus 2:18 names Reuel as the father of the seven daughters.
Exodus 3:1 explicitly calls Jethro Moses' father-in-law and the priest of Midian.
The most straightforward reading is that Reuel and Jethro refer to the same man, perhaps reflecting multiple names or a name and title.
However, some interpreters have suggested different family relationships, partly because biblical kinship terminology and later references to Hobab raise questions about how the names fit together.
Numbers 10:29 and Judges 4:11 contribute to that discussion.
Scripture does not provide a complete family genealogy resolving every difficulty.
So we should not pretend that it does.
But the central account is clear.
Moses entered the household of a Midianite priest.
And that household became part of God's providential preparation for Israel's future deliverer.
When the daughters explained why they had returned so quickly, they said an Egyptian had rescued them from the shepherds and had even drawn water for their flock.
An Egyptian.
That was how they identified Moses.
They did not yet know the full story of the man who had helped them.
They did not know about the basket in the Nile.
They did not know about Pharaoh's palace.
They did not know about the dead Egyptian hidden in the sand.
They did not know that the man standing at the well would one day lead Israel out of slavery.
They simply knew that someone had helped them.
And their father responded with a question that changed the direction of Moses' life.
“Where is he?”
Then came another question.
“Why have ye left the man?”
And finally, the invitation.
“Call him, that he may eat bread.”
Those words come from Exodus 2:20 in the King James Version.
Do not rush past them.
A fugitive was being invited to a table.
A stranger was being welcomed into a household.
A man who had lost his place in Egypt was being offered hospitality in Midian.
We are not told everything Jethro knew about Moses at that moment.
We are not told that he recognized Moses' divine calling.
We are not told that he had received a prophecy about him.
What Scripture actually records is simpler.
He learned that a stranger had helped his daughters.
And he invited that stranger to eat.
Sometimes the actions that matter most in someone's life do not look spectacular when they happen.
Sometimes they look like making room at a table.
Offering food.
Recognizing kindness.
Giving a displaced person a place to stay.
And while the passage does not explicitly describe Jethro's inner motives, his recorded actions show hospitality toward the man who had helped his family.
There is a lesson here that reaches beyond the ancient world.
We often want to participate in something great for God.
We imagine dramatic moments.
Crowds.
Platforms.
Public victories.
A calling that everyone can recognize.
But what if an important act of faithfulness is much quieter?
What if it is the person you welcome when they have nowhere to go?
The exhausted believer you encourage.
The stranger you treat with dignity.
The struggling family member you refuse to discard.
The wounded person you listen to instead of judging immediately.
You may never know how God will use an ordinary act of mercy.
Jethro did not need to know Moses' entire future to extend hospitality.
And Moses did not need to understand his entire calling to accept it.
Exodus 2:21 then tells us:
“And Moses was content to dwell with the man: and he gave Moses Zipporah his daughter.”
That one verse contains an enormous transition.
Moses went from fleeing for his life to settling in Midian.
From being a stranger at a well to becoming part of a household.
From isolation to marriage.
From the ruins of one chapter into the beginning of another.
But we must be careful not to turn this into a sentimental story in which every wound instantly disappears.
The Bible does not say Moses forgot Egypt.
It does not say his past no longer troubled him.
It does not say life in Midian was free from hardship.
In fact, the name of his first son reveals that displacement remained part of his identity.
Exodus 2:22 records Moses naming his son Gershom, explaining that he had been a stranger in a foreign land.
Even while building a family, Moses remembered that he was far from home.
And perhaps some of you understand that feeling more deeply than you can explain.
You can be surrounded by people and still feel displaced.
You can have a job and still feel that you have lost your purpose.
You can sit at a dinner table and still carry grief nobody sees.
You can smile in a family photograph while privately wondering how your life became so different from what you imagined.
Moses was living.
Working.
Building a family.
But Egypt was still part of his story.
And the cries of Israel had not disappeared.
Then Exodus 3:1 reveals another important detail about Jethro.
The Hebrew begins:
וּמֹשֶׁה הָיָה רֹעֶה אֶת־צֹאן יִתְרוֹ חֹתְנוֹ כֹּהֵן מִדְיָן
Umosheh hayah roʿeh et-tson Yitro hoteno kohen Midyan.
A close translation is:
“Now Moses was shepherding the flock of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of Midian.”
There it is.
Jethro.
יִתְרוֹ (Yitrō).
The man previously introduced through his daughters and household is now named as Moses' father-in-law.
And Moses is caring for his flock.
Think about the contrast.
Moses had once lived in Pharaoh's household.
Now he was tending sheep belonging to his father-in-law.
The man who had known the world of Egyptian power was learning the rhythms of wilderness life.
The future leader of Israel was working as a shepherd.
And the biblical narrative places him in that ordinary occupation immediately before the extraordinary encounter at the burning bush.
We should not claim that Scripture explicitly says Jethro personally trained Moses in every leadership skill he would later need.
It does not.
But we can see that Moses' years in Midian were not empty years.
He lived in Jethro's household.
He became a husband and father.
He worked as a shepherd.
He became familiar with the wilderness.
And it was while shepherding Jethro's flock that he came to Horeb, the mountain of God.
There the LORD appeared to him in the flame of fire from the midst of a bush.
A bush that burned.
But was not consumed.
And suddenly the shepherd who had fled Egypt heard his name.
“Moses, Moses.”
The man who had been hiding from Pharaoh was now standing on holy ground before the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
God had seen the affliction of His people.
God had heard their cry.
God knew their suffering.
And God was sending Moses back to Egypt.
Not because Moses had become flawless.
Not because his past had been morally insignificant.
Not because his own strength was enough.
But because the LORD had chosen to act in faithfulness to His covenant.
When Moses questioned his ability, God's answer was not a speech about Moses' greatness.
It was a promise of divine presence.
“Certainly I will be with thee.”
Exodus 3:12, KJV.
That is the center of the calling.
Not Moses' confidence.
God's presence.
And this is where we must understand something essential about the difference between biblical redemption and motivational storytelling.
The message is not that every broken person is secretly destined to become famous.
The message is not that your failures automatically qualify you for leadership.
The message is not that God approves of whatever you did because He can still bring good out of your life.
The message is that the living God is sovereign, merciful, holy, and able to accomplish His purposes through people whose histories are far from perfect.
Moses needed God.
Israel needed God.
And we need God.
But Jethro's story does not end with Moses leaving Midian.
In Exodus 4:18, Moses returned to his father-in-law, there called Jether, a related form of the name, and asked permission to return to his relatives in Egypt.
Jethro answered:
“Go in peace.”
That is another remarkable moment.
The man who had received Moses into his household was now watching him depart.
The shepherd was leaving the flock.
The son-in-law was returning to the land from which he had fled.
And Jethro's recorded response was peaceful permission.
Later, in Exodus 18, Jethro returned to the center of the narrative.
By then, the LORD had delivered Israel from Egypt.
The Red Sea had been crossed.
The power of Pharaoh had been broken.
And Jethro heard what God had done for Moses and His people.
Exodus 18:9 tells us that Jethro rejoiced over the good the LORD had done for Israel.
Then he made an extraordinary declaration.
The Hebrew of Exodus 18:11 begins:
עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי־גָדוֹל יְהוָה מִכָּל־הָאֱלֹהִים
Attah yadaʿti ki-gadol Adonai mikkol-haʾelohim.
A close translation is:
“Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods.”

In the Hebrew text, the divine name is represented by the four letters יהוה, commonly called the Tetragrammaton. Adonai is the traditional Jewish reverential reading used in place of pronouncing that name.
Now consider the significance.
The priest of Midian was rejoicing over the deliverance accomplished by the LORD.
He was acknowledging the LORD's supremacy.
He offered sacrifices to God.
And Aaron and the elders of Israel shared a meal with him before God.
This is powerful.
But again, precision matters.
Does this prove that Jethro had been an idolater who converted at that exact moment?
Not conclusively.
The declaration certainly demonstrates a profound acknowledgment of the LORD's greatness, and many interpreters understand it as evidence of a decisive religious response.
But Scripture does not give us a complete account of Jethro's beliefs before meeting Moses.
We should celebrate what the text reveals without claiming certainty about what it leaves hidden.
And then comes another extraordinary moment.
Jethro watched Moses attempting to judge the disputes of the people from morning until evening.
He recognized a serious problem.
Moses was carrying too much responsibility alone.
The people were waiting.
The leader was exhausting himself.
And the system was unsustainable.
Jethro confronted the problem directly.
“The thing that thou doest is not good.”
Exodus 18:17, KJV.
Imagine hearing that.
Moses had stood before Pharaoh.
Moses had witnessed the plagues.
Moses had led Israel through the sea.
Yet his father-in-law could still look at his leadership and say:
This is not good.
You cannot keep doing everything yourself.
Jethro advised Moses to teach the people God's statutes and laws while appointing capable, trustworthy leaders to handle ordinary disputes.
More difficult matters could then come to Moses.
But Jethro did not present his counsel as though his own wisdom outranked God's authority.
In Exodus 18:23, he explicitly conditioned his recommendation on God's command.
And Moses listened.
This is one of the most beautiful and challenging details in the account.
The great deliverer of Israel was willing to receive practical correction from his father-in-law.
He did not need to pretend he had every answer.
He did not need to defend an exhausting system simply because he had created it.
He could listen.
He could learn.
He could change.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that more than anything else.
You can love God and still need correction.
You can be called to serve and still need wisdom from another person.
You can be sincere and still be doing something in an unhealthy way.
You can have genuine spiritual responsibility and still need rest, boundaries, and help.
Not every warning is an attack.
Not every correction is rejection.
Sometimes the person who cares about you is the one willing to tell you that the way you are living cannot continue.
Some parents are exhausted because they believe they must carry every burden alone.
Some pastors are collapsing because they cannot delegate.
Some believers are spiritually drained because they confuse constant activity with faithfulness.
Some families are quietly suffering because one person refuses to admit that help is needed.
Jethro's counsel reminds us that humility is not weakness.
And receiving wise counsel is not the same as abandoning faith.
But there is an even deeper question.
Why does this story matter to followers of Jesus Christ?
Because the Bible is not ultimately a collection of inspiring personalities for us to admire.
It is the unfolding testimony of God's redemptive purposes, culminating in Jesus Christ.
Moses was a real historical figure within the biblical narrative, called by God to lead Israel out of slavery.
But the New Testament also shows us that Moses' ministry points beyond himself.
Deuteronomy 18:15 speaks of a prophet whom God would raise up.
In Acts 3:22–26, Peter connects that promise to the work of Jesus Christ.
And Hebrews 3:1–6 draws a profound distinction between Moses and Jesus.
Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house.
Christ is faithful as the Son over God's house.
Moses led a people out of bondage in Egypt.
Jesus accomplishes a greater redemption from sin and death.
Moses mediated the old covenant.
Jesus is the mediator of the new covenant, established through His sacrificial death.
And while Jethro's hospitality helped provide a home for Moses during his years in Midian, the ultimate hope of the Gospel is not that we might find a comfortable place in this world.
It is that through Jesus Christ, sinners can be reconciled to God.
That is where this story becomes personal.
Because there is something worse than losing a palace.
Something worse than losing status.
Something worse than being misunderstood by people.
It is being separated from God by sin.
And no amount of religious performance can repair that separation.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
You cannot earn salvation through donations.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that unmistakably clear.
And the same passage teaches that those saved by grace are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
The order matters.
Grace first.
Then the grateful life that grace produces.
Not payment for salvation.
Not bargaining for divine favor.
Not trying to make God love us more.
But responding to the love already revealed in Christ.
Romans 5:8 tells us that God demonstrated His love toward us while we were still sinners, through the death of Christ.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus did not come merely to inspire damaged people to become more successful versions of themselves.
He came to save sinners.
He lived without sin.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
And He calls us to repentance and faith.
The same God who did not abandon His covenant people in Egypt has revealed His saving mercy through His Son.
And when we speak of going from scandal to grace, we must never pretend that grace means sin was harmless.
Sin is serious enough that the Son of God went to the cross.
Grace is glorious enough that forgiveness is offered to sinners through Him.
Maybe your scandal was public.
Maybe people know exactly what happened.
Maybe they still mention your name when they talk about failure.
Or maybe your scandal is private.
The thoughts you hide.
The resentment you feed.
The secret compromises.
The dishonesty.
The spiritual coldness beneath your religious appearance.
The prayers you stopped praying because you felt too ashamed to approach God.
And perhaps you have become so skilled at looking strong that nobody knows how exhausted you are.
But Jesus knows.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not to continue pretending.
It is to come into the light.
To confess.
To repent.
To trust the Savior who died and rose again.
First John 1:9 assures believers of God's faithfulness and righteousness in forgiving confessed sins and cleansing from unrighteousness.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
Moses' history did not vanish.
Neither do all the consequences of ours.
But forgiveness in Christ is real.
And a life surrendered to Him can truly change.
So look again at the well in Midian.
A stranger sitting beside it.
Seven daughters coming for water.
A priest waiting at home.
A simple invitation to eat.
A household that would become part of Moses' wilderness years.
A flock that Moses would later shepherd.
A mountain where God would speak.
A nation that would be delivered.
And a father-in-law who would eventually rejoice in the LORD's greatness and offer wisdom to a weary leader.
Not one of those moments gives us permission to invent Jethro's hidden past.
But together, they show us that God was working through ordinary human relationships while accomplishing His extraordinary purposes.
And here is something I do not want you to miss.
Jethro did not need to be the central figure in the Exodus to have a meaningful place in the story.
He was not Moses.
He was not Aaron.
He was not the one standing before Pharaoh.
But he welcomed, provided a household connection, and later gave counsel that Moses received.
There are people who will never stand before a crowd.
Never preach to thousands.
Never have their names remembered by history.
Yet their hospitality, encouragement, wisdom, prayers, and faithful service may strengthen someone God is using.
That does not make them less valuable.
The kingdom of God is not built on celebrity.
And the worth of a disciple is not measured by visibility.
Perhaps you are not called to be Moses.
Perhaps you are called to be faithful where God has placed you.
To open a door.
To offer a meal.
To speak truth with love.
To support someone who is weary.
To help another believer remain grounded in Scripture.
To teach your children the Gospel.
To encourage a struggling friend to return to Christ.
And perhaps you are the one sitting at the well right now.
Displaced.
Ashamed.
Uncertain.
Wondering whether anything good can still come from your life.
Please remember this.
Moses did not know what awaited him when he sat beside that well.
He did not know the burning bush was ahead.
He did not know how God would confront Pharaoh.
He did not know the sea would open.
And he certainly did not know how his story would be remembered.
He only knew the life he had left behind.
But God knew the rest.
That does not mean you are guaranteed an extraordinary public calling.
It means your future is not beyond God's knowledge, and your failures do not place you beyond the reach of His mercy.
Do not confuse a painful chapter with the final verdict on your life.
And do not confuse waiting with God's absence.
If this story has exposed something you have been carrying, I want to invite you to respond with spiritual honesty.
You do not need to disclose private details to strangers.
You do not need to perform your pain publicly.
But there is something beautiful about a community where people can acknowledge their need for God's mercy and pray for one another.
And if this message reminds you of someone who feels forgotten, consider sharing it with them.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to pressure them.
But to remind them that God's Word still speaks into ordinary lives.
And if you have been strengthened by this ministry, I also want to speak to you about something that matters to our mission.
Gospel Warrior exists to help people encounter the truth of Scripture, understand the Gospel, and grow in their relationship with Jesus Christ.
This work requires time, resources, consistency, and faithful support.
Every article shared, every person encouraged, every resource made accessible, and every effort to expand our reach is part of a mission we want to continue with integrity.
We want these resources to remain available to people who need biblical nourishment, including those who cannot afford to pay.
And that is one reason voluntary support matters.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful, not compelled by guilt or pressure (2 Corinthians 9:7).
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, worship, generosity, and a life shaped by grace.
You would not be buying God's favor.
You would be helping sustain a ministry that seeks to proclaim His Word.
These items are simply an expression of appreciation. They are not the reason we proclaim the Gospel, and they are not a measure of anyone's spiritual commitment.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
More Scripture.
More biblical teaching.
More resources for people who are spiritually hungry.
More opportunities to encourage those who are struggling.
More people being invited to hear the good news of Jesus Christ.
Keep reading.
Keep growing.
Keep praying.
Keep sharing the truth.
Your presence and your faithfulness matter beyond any financial contribution.
Because this was never meant to be about building a platform around a personality.
It must always be about pointing people to the Person who alone can save.
Jesus Christ.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who forgives.
The One who restores.
The One who transforms.
The One whose grace is greater than our ability to rescue ourselves.
And when we return to Jethro, perhaps the most fitting conclusion is not to turn him into a hero the Bible never claims he was.
It is to appreciate the role Scripture actually gives him.
A priest of Midian.
A father of seven daughters.
A man also called Reuel.
A host to Moses.
The father of Zipporah.
The owner of the flock Moses tended.
A witness to God's deliverance.
A man who rejoiced in the LORD's greatness.
And a father-in-law whose counsel helped Moses recognize the need for shared responsibility.
He did not need a manufactured past to make his story worth telling.
And you do not need a manufactured testimony to make God's mercy meaningful in your life.
You do not have to exaggerate your suffering.
You do not have to make your past sound worse than it was.
You do not have to pretend your restoration is complete when God is still working on your heart.
Just tell the truth.
Tell the truth about your sin.
Tell the truth about your need.
Tell the truth about the grace of Jesus Christ.
And when you fall, do not make peace with sin.
Return to the Savior.
When you are corrected, do not let pride keep you from listening.
Receive what is true.
When someone is suffering, do not wait until you know their entire story before showing compassion.
Love your neighbor.
When God gives you an opportunity to serve, do not despise it because it looks ordinary.
Be faithful.
And when you look at your past and wonder whether your life can still become something beautiful in God's hands, remember the fugitive who sat beside a well in Midian.
His story was not finished.
But more importantly, remember the Savior who died and rose again so that sinners could receive forgiveness and new life.
Because our ultimate hope is not that we can become another Moses.
Our hope is that we belong to Jesus Christ.
The chapter you are most ashamed of does not have to be the final word—because the cross has already spoken a greater word of mercy to everyone who comes to Christ.
